name: Molecular gastronomy
region: Roses in Catalonia and Bray in England
summary: A kitchen that uses the science of food as a tool and a game. Hervé This and Nicholas Kurti named the field in 1988. Ferran Adrià at elBulli and Heston Blumenthal at The Fat Duck made foams, spheres and liquid-nitrogen ice cream.

philosophy.core_thesis: Cooks can ask why food changes when it is heated, mixed or frozen, and then use the answer to build new textures, temperatures and surprises.
design_principles: Ask a physical or chemical question about a dish, test it in the kitchen, and keep the answer.
Change the form of the ingredient: a liquid becomes a sphere, a purée becomes a foam, a cream becomes a powder.
Keep the taste of the ingredient clear while its texture and temperature change.
Play with the senses: serve hot and cold in one bite, and add sound, smell or a story to the dish.
Cook slowly at an exact low temperature, and measure the heat with a probe.
Serve a long sequence of small courses as one show, with each course a new surprise.
Work in a research kitchen, record each test, and share the findings.
anti_patterns: A trick that has no taste of the ingredient
A heavy classic sauce that hides the texture
A dish that comes from habit, not from a question
A menu of familiar courses in the usual order
A rustic plate that hides the technique
A chemical effect that the guest cannot see or taste

plating.composition: A small, exact object or a group of objects on a clean surface: a sphere, a foam or a frozen piece, placed with a spoon or in a special vessel.
plating.plate: A white plate, a glass or a spoon, a slate or a vessel made for one dish: a petri dish, a tube or a bag.
plating.portion: Twenty to thirty-five courses of 5 to 40 g each; a main piece of 60 g at most.
plating.height: Low or very small: a sphere of 20 mm, a foam in a glass of 60 mm, a frozen dish that gives off vapour.
rules: Serve each course in the vessel that fits its form: a spoon for a sphere, a glass for a foam.
Place one clear object on a clean surface and leave most of the plate empty.
Serve the cold and the hot parts at the last second, so that the temperature contrast stays.
Use a surprise of form: a food that looks like another food.
Give the order of the bites to the guest, and explain it in one short line.

pantry.rule: Take each ingredient as a source of flavour, and use the gels, thickeners and gases of the laboratory to change its form.

technique.bases: Alginate and calcium baths, agar and xanthan gels, lecithin air, nitrous-oxide foams and low-temperature water baths.
technique.details: A sphere that bursts in the mouth, a warm gel, a frozen powder, an air of lecithin, a drop of oil in a gel.

flavour.profile: Clear, bright and surprising: the taste of one ingredient in a strange form.
flavour.balance: Each bite has one lead taste, a clear acid or sweet note, and a contrast of temperature.
flavour.fat: Light fats in small parts: oils in gels and airs, cream in foams; 15 to 30 per cent of the energy of a course.
flavour.seasoning: Salt in a flake or a spray, lemon, herbs and spices in oils, airs and powders.

palette.strategy: Use clean, pure colours of the ingredients on white, so that the form of the food, not the colour, gives the surprise.

service.format: A long tasting menu of small courses that the cooks explain at the table, with a few courses served in front of the guest.
service.courses: Twenty to thirty-five small courses, in the form of a show, with snacks, a tasting sequence and a long run of desserts.
service.tableware: Special vessels made for single dishes: spoons, glass, tubes, tongs and bags, with plain white china for the rest.
service.setting: A plain dining room by the sea or in a village, with an open or a glass-walled kitchen and a calm, theatrical service.

dishes.dish: Bacon and egg ice cream, frozen at the table
Salmon cooked at a low temperature in a liquorice gel
Sound of the Sea: seafood on edible sand, with a sea sound

positive: a spherical olive on a spoon
one exact object on the plate

canonical_works.maker: Ferran Adrià, Juli Soler and Albert Adrià

canonical_works.work: Molecular Gastronomy: Exploring the Science of Flavor

evidence.title: Liquid nitrogen delivery at The Fat Duck, Bray
El Bulli on Cala Montjoi, Roses

emotion.target_response: The surprise of a magic trick that you can taste: a food that is not what it looks like.

use_cases: a tasting menu that plays with texture and temperature
a food photograph of a sphere, a foam or a frozen dish
a menu that tells a science story
avoid_when: the brief wants simple, local or foraged food
the brief wants a rich classic sauce
the brief is home or street food

modifiers.request: more rigour and more recipes in a book
modifiers.how: Keep the methods; measure them, publish the times and temperatures, and use the plate as a clean, exact page.

modifiers.request: return to the land and the season
modifiers.how: Remove gels and foams; use wild plants, ferments and wood fire, and serve on stoneware.
